applied.problem: Overstated absolutes: random errors 'never' cancel fully (a mean of four can land exactly on 27.00 V); a reading 'easily' lands 0.08 V out (2 SD, about 1 in 20); the 1/√n rule needs independent errors; accuracy is not always %+digits; 'the meter is still within its accuracy' asserts an unstated spe…

Worked example says the true voltage 'could be anywhere' in a 95%-plus straight-sum bracket; the standard method combines in quadrature, so this is a cautious bracket. More readings cannot help when the accuracy part dominates, as here. Pass/fail rules vary by job; no safety line on a live battery.
Screen 7 says accuracy is written as a percentage of the reading plus digits as if always so; the source says accuracy 'may' include digits, and some meters state it otherwise.

notes.problem: 'Confidence of a doubled bracket, 95%' cites source 1, whose quote gives a 95% example but does not say that ±2 standard errors gives 95%; it is textbook-certain only for many readings (about 95.4% for a normal pile).
'Readings below which textbooks raise the factor, about 30' is a textbook rule of thumb (the t-distribution), kept as assumed; no research source states it.
